content.title: About
content.content: Almonds are the edible seeds of the almond tree (Prunus dulcis), native to the Middle East and Central Asia and now grown in many warm regions worldwide. They have a mild, slightly sweet, nutty flavor and a crunchy texture. Almonds are eaten raw, roasted, or blanched and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and almond milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almonds are related to peaches, plums, and cherries; the almond itself is the seed inside the fruit's pit.
Sweet almonds are the ones eaten as food; bitter almonds contain toxic compounds and are not sold as ordinary snacks.
Almond trees have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Almonds are used to make almond flour, almond butter, marzipan, and almond milk.
Almond blossoms appear in early spring, before the leaves.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Almonds are one of the best food sources of vitamin E, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Almonds contain mostly monounsaturated fats, which can be part of a heart‑friendly diet.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Almonds contribute plant protein and fiber, which support fullness.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Almonds contain more calcium than most other nuts.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Almonds can cause allergic reactions, which may be severe in some people.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Almonds are calorie‑dense, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole almonds are not suitable for young children because they can cause choking.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Almonds contain oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit. Bitter almonds should never be eaten raw.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Almonds can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, salads, and baked goods, or ground into almond flour and almond butter. Soaking or blanching softens them and makes the skins easy to remove. Unsalted or lightly salted almonds are a good option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store almonds in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer, since their oils can turn rancid. Discard almonds that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.

content.title: About
content.content: Carrot cake or cupcake is a baked good whose base includes grated carrot, giving it moisture, a subtle sweet flavor, and a characteristic orange hue. The batter typically contains flour, sugar, eggs, vegetable oil, and warm spices such as cinnamon, ginger, and nutmeg. Often walnuts, raisins, or pineapple are added, and the cake is finished with a cream cheese frosting.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrot cake became popular in the United States in the 1970s as a way to add natural sweetness and moisture to baked goods.
Grated carrot retains a high amount of beta‑carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.
The classic cream cheese frosting was first popularized in New York carrot‑cake recipes.
Carrot cupcakes are often marketed as a healthier alternative to overly sweet desserts because the carrot adds natural sweetness and nutrients.
In some cultures carrot cake is associated with spring celebrations, its bright color symbolizing the awakening of nature.

items.title: Beta‑carotene and Vitamin A
items.content: Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: Grated carrot adds both soluble and insoluble fiber to the batter, aiding digestion and promoting satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Spices like cinnamon and ginger contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Lower Glycemic Impact
items.content: The fiber content and moderate sugar level give carrot cake a lower glycemic index than many other sweets.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Carrot cake provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, essential for normal bodily functions.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Traditional recipes contain a notable amount of sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Nut Allergies
items.content: If walnuts or other nuts are added, they can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: The oil and cream cheese frosting make the cake relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Standard recipes use wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for gluten‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve carrot cake or cupcake at room temperature, often topped with cream cheese frosting. Slice into portions and enjoy with tea or coffee, or serve as a dessert after a meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Individual portions can be frozen in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months; thaw in the refrigerator before serving.

chicken-breast-rotisserie-skin-not-eaten.title: Chicken Breast, Rotisserie, Skin Not Eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Rotisserie chicken breast without skin is a lean source of protein. The rotisserie method keeps the meat juicy while the removal of skin reduces fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rotisserie chicken breast is a staple in fast‑food outlets and cafeterias because it cooks quickly.
Removing the skin cuts the calorie count by roughly 30 % compared with skin‑on breast.
Chicken meat is rich in vitamin B6, which plays a role in amino‑acid metabolism.
Proper rotisserie cooking creates a golden crust that adds flavor without added fat.
Chicken breast is one of the most consumed proteins in weight‑loss diets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast contains less than 2 g of fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B3 and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: The combination of protein and low fat helps maintain and build lean muscle.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; ensure the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content in prepared products
items.content: Pre‑seasoned rotisserie breasts often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the breast and add it to salads, sandwiches, pasta dishes, or use it as a base for Asian‑style stir‑fries. It can be quickly reheated in a microwave or skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it retains quality for 2‑3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Gumbo with rice is a classic Creole stew consisting of a thick, flavorful broth made with seafood, meat (often chicken or sausage), vegetables, and a blend of aromatic spices, served over steamed rice. The dish combines the culinary influences of Louisiana, the Caribbean, and the American South.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gumbo originated in New Orleans in the early 19th century as a fusion of French, Spanish, African, and Native American cooking traditions.
Traditional gumbo is thickened with a dark roux or with filé powder (ground sassafras leaves), though many modern recipes skip the filé.
The “holy trinity” of Cajun/Creole cooking—onion, celery, and bell pepper—is the aromatic base for every gumbo.
Gumbo is often cooked in large kettles and served at festivals, community gatherings, and family celebrations.
It is considered the unofficial state dish of Louisiana and is part of the United States’ culinary heritage.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Seafood and meat provide complete, high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair and growth.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The broth and spices supply thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Sausage and shellfish contribute iron, which is vital for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables (onion, celery, pepper) and rice add fiber that promotes digestive health.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Cayenne, paprika, and garlic contain polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Gumbo often includes shrimp, crab, or oysters, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared broths and seasoning mixes can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Cayenne and black pepper may irritate the stomach of those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Seafood must be fully cooked; undercooked ingredients can harbor harmful bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve gumbo hot, ladling it over a bed of steamed rice. Garnish with chopped parsley or green onions and a squeeze of lemon for brightness. Leftovers keep well in the fridge and can be reheated gently on the stove, adding a splash of broth to restore moisture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover gumbo in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. When reheating, bring the stew to a rolling boil to ensure safety.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon juice, 100 % freshly squeezed, is obtained from ripe lemons without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright, refreshing taste and characteristic aroma, retaining most of the vitamins and minerals of the original fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemons are among the oldest cultivated citrus fruits – they have been grown for over 2,500 years.
Freshly squeezed juice retains up to 90 % of vitamin C, which degrades quickly with heat.
Lemon juice is often used as a natural preservative in cooking because of its acidity (pH ≈ 2.5).
The juice helps improve iron absorption from plant foods.
In traditional medicine, lemon juice is used to support digestion and detoxification.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Acids in the juice stimulate gastric juice production, enhancing food breakdown.

items.title: Improves iron absorption
items.content: Ascorbic acid increases the bioavailability of non‑heme iron from plant sources.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Besides vitamin C, the juice contains flavonoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The juice is almost entirely water, helping maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent consumption of acidic drinks may contribute to enamel erosion; rinsing the mouth with water afterward is recommended.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to citrus fruits.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: The acids in lemon juice can affect the absorption of certain drugs, such as some antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon juice can be added to water, tea, sauces, marinades, baked goods and desserts. It is commonly used as a salad dressing or to make lemonade. If desired, dilute the juice with water in a 1:4 ratio for a milder flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed bottle for no more than 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze it in portioned ice cubes. Discard the juice if its color changes, it develops an off‑smell, or sediment appears.

peas-and-carrots-canned-cooked-no-added-.title: Peas and carrots, canned, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots canned are a ready‑to‑eat vegetable mix that has been cooked and sealed in airtight jars without any added fat. The product retains most of the nutrients of the fresh vegetables and is convenient for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning allows vegetables to be stored for several years while preserving flavor and color.
Peas are high in plant protein and fiber, while carrots provide provitamin A (beta‑carotene).
In many countries these cans are common in school meals and backpacking rations.
The jars are typically heat‑treated at 115 °C for 30‑45 minutes to ensure safety.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Peas deliver about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good meat alternative for vegetarians.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots converts to vitamin A, essential for vision and immune function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes this product suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned vegetables are often salted for preservation; people monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to peas; discontinue use if symptoms appear.

items.title: Bacterial safety
items.content: Bulging or damaged cans can indicate bacterial growth; such products should be discarded.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the jar: add it to soups, stews, salads, pasta, or serve as a side dish. It can be warmed briefly in the microwave or on the stovetop if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3‑4 days.

taco-flour-tortilla-pork-cheese.title: Flour Tortilla Taco with Pork and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A flour tortilla filled with tender pork and melted cheese is a classic Mexican fast‑food item. The tortilla is soft and pliable, while the seasoned pork and cheese create a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flour tortillas originated in northern Mexico in the 19th century as an alternative to corn tortillas.
Pork is usually marinated in chili, cumin and lime before being grilled or pan‑fried.
The cheese used is often a melty cheddar or Mexican "queso fresco".
Tortillas can be served soft or crisp, depending on the cooking method.
Traditional toppings include salsa, guacamole and fresh cilantro.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Pork and cheese provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Cheese is a good source of calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Red meat contains readily absorbable heme iron, vital for blood formation.

items.title: Dietary fiber (in the tortilla)
items.content: A flour tortilla adds a modest amount of fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Cheese and pork can be high in saturated fat, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese is often salty, contributing to higher sodium intake.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy should avoid the cheese component.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A taco with meat and cheese is calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the tortilla on a skillet or grill, add cooked pork, sprinkle with shredded cheese, and top with fresh vegetables, salsa, guacamole or sour cream as desired. Fold or roll the tortilla to eat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Keep tortillas in a dry place, and keep meat and cheese refrigerated. Reheat before serving in a microwave or skillet.

turkey-or-chicken-sausage-reduced-sodium.title: Turkey or Chicken Sausage, Reduced Sodium (1000)

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey or chicken sausage with reduced sodium (1000 mg per serving) is a lean meat product made from white poultry meat, seasoned with spices and a minimal amount of salt. It is suitable for those who monitor sodium intake but still want the taste of sausage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey and chicken contain less saturated fat than traditional pork sausage.
Reducing sodium to 1000 mg helps lower the risk of high blood pressure.
The product is often used in diet plans focused on low‑salt consumption.
Cold smoking is used in the process, preserving juiciness and flavor.
It can be produced without artificial preservatives.

items.title: Low Sodium Content
items.content: Reduced salt supports healthy blood pressure levels.

items.title: Rich Source of Protein
items.content: A serving provides about 15‑20 g of high‑quality protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Low Fat
items.content: The sausage contains less saturated fat, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry meat is high in niacin and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Selenium Content
items.content: Selenium contributes to the body’s antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Poultry Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey or chicken.

items.title: Nitrite Content
items.content: Certain versions may contain small amounts of nitrites as preservatives.

items.title: Processed Meat
items.content: As with any processed meat, it should be consumed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sausage can be eaten cold in sandwiches, sliced into salads, added to omelets, or quickly pan‑heated. It pairs well with whole‑grain bread, mustard, and fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container. After opening, use within 5‑7 days. When frozen, quality is maintained for up to 2 months.
